processing: As with other Wuyi rock teas: withered, shaken, partly oxidised, rolled and roasted.
harvest_season: Not documented in detail; Wuyi rock teas are normally picked in spring.
appearance_dry: Typical of Wuyi rock teas: dark, twisted strips.
appearance_liquor: Typical of roasted Wuyi oolongs: clear orange to amber.
appearance_wet: Typical of the class: green-brown leaves with darker edges.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record was published for it. Its Tie Guan Yin parentage and name point towards aroma, but expect mainly the roast and mineral weight typical of the class.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for Wuyi rock teas: hot water and short steeps.

vintage_note: How it is sold is not well documented. As is usual for Wuyi rock teas, expect harvest-year and roast labelling, and possibly the number 101 in place of the name.
description:
Yue Ming Xiang is a modern bred cultivar known by the number 101 in lists of rock-tea varieties, with Tie Guan Yin given as a parent. It is one of the less familiar names in that series.

Little is written about how it behaves in the making, so assume the class method: shaking, partial oxidation and roasting.

Tasting descriptions are hard to come by. Brew it hot and short, and look for whatever aroma its parentage might give, without expecting it to taste like Anxi Tie Guan Yin.

If you see it on sale, ask for the year, the roast and the growing area, since this is not a name most buyers can judge on reputation.
history: A list of Fujian-bred rock-tea cultivars gives it code 101, Tie Guan Yin as parent and a publication year of 1994. Beyond that, little is documented about who selected it or how widely it spread.
